description:
I’ve loved space since I was a kid, staring at the stars and dreaming that one day people would walk on Mars, wishing I could be part of it somehow.
Now I’m a third year AI student, and this challenge feels like my chance. I’m building a map for the first astronauts there. It uses NASA data and AI to find safe paths and places worth exploring.
I probably won’t be the one walking on Mars. But if something I build guides those first footsteps, even a little, that would mean everything to me.
summary:
First Martian Sol is a Marswalk planner for the first astronauts on Mars. When a crew steps outside, they have limited oxygen, hard terrain, patchy radio and no rescue team. First Martian Sol plans that walk before they leave, then guides them during it.

It works on one real place: a 2.4 × 2.8 km site on Mount Sharp, Gale Crater, explored by NASA's Curiosity rover. Seven NASA data sources are layered on that site, and an AI model trained on NASA JPL's AI4Mars dataset finds loose sand in Curiosity's photos, which orbit cannot see well. Every stop is checked for steep ground, loose sand, radio line of sight and the time to walk home, with a clear go, go-with-cautions or no-go verdict. Outside, a helmet display guides the walk live, with a printable briefing card as backup.

It matters because every first step on Mars needs a map, so everyone who steps out comes home.
details:
First Martian Sol answers one question for the first crew on Mars: where can we walk safely, and how do we get home? The crew places stops on a real map, or lets the data suggest science stops (for example, ground where orbit sees clays). The planner finds a route a suited astronaut can actually walk, checks every stop, and explains every risk in plain words. If a stop is in loose sand, out of radio contact or too far from home, its pin turns amber or red and the plan says why. The verdict uses mission-control language: go, go with cautions, or no-go.


How it works
- A real site: The boxwork region on Mount Sharp, Gale Crater (4.8° S, 137.4° E), 2.4 × 2.8 km, where Curiosity has been exploring.
- Seven NASA data sources: HiRISE photo (25 cm), 1 m elevation model, CRISM minerals, THEMIS day and night temperatures, Curiosity's REMS weather, RAD radiation, and 46,587 of Curiosity's own photos. Each layer shows its pixel size, so a coarse layer is never trusted like a sharp one.
- A walking model for a suited astronaut: Pace and metabolic rate follow the Santee model used in MIT's SEXTANT EVA planner, capped at NASA's 352 W suit design rate (BVAD 2022). Oxygen use and radiation dose follow from that.
- Safety fields over the whole site: Minutes to walk home from anywhere, radio line of sight to the habitat, radiation shelter from terrain, and sunlight and shadow at any time of sol (Mars24 sun model).
- An AI terrain model: A U-Net (ResNet-34 encoder) trained on 5,303 labelled Curiosity photos from NASA JPL's AI4Mars dataset. On 277 photos it had never seen, it reached 98.5% pixel accuracy (mean IoU 0.81). It then read 486 Navcam photos from the 162 Curiosity stops in the site. Where it finds deep sand, the route avoids it or warns about the crossing, and every stop shows the real photo next to the model's reading.


- Three displays for three moments: A planning screen in the habitat; a helmet display that guides the walk live (heading, turn guidance, oxygen, suit time, cautions); and a one-page briefing card, black on white, as a backup if the display or radio fails, like the checklists Apollo astronauts wore on their sleeves. See the helmet display and the briefing card below.


Checked against NASA data
- Our elevation map vs Curiosity's own recorded heights at 164 stops: typical difference 0.12 m (mean +0.01 m).
- Our sun model vs REMS sunrise and sunset: within half a degree.
- Oxygen conversion: 0.074 kg/h at 300 W vs NASA BVAD 0.075 kg/h at 293 W.
- Radiation: 6 hours outside gives 160 µSv, matching RAD's 0.64 mSv per day.


Benefits and who could use it
Mission planners preparing crewed EVAs; crews and controllers in Mars simulation habitats on Earth; and, with lunar data in place of the Mars layers, EVA planning for Artemis on the Moon. Because it runs in any browser on open data, it can also teach students how a Mars walk is planned.


It's creative because
- It plans for people, not rovers: Most Mars maps are built for driving. First Martian Sol measures the ground in footsteps, oxygen and minutes to walk home, using published models of a suited astronaut.
- It joins orbit and ground: Orbit cannot see loose sand well, but Curiosity's photos can. An AI model reads those photos and its reading changes the route, so the two views of Mars work together.
- It speaks like mission control: Every plan ends in go, go with cautions or no-go, and every warning is a plain sentence, not just a colour.
- One plan, three moments: The same plan becomes a planning screen in the habitat, a live helmet display during the walk, and a paper card as backup, inspired by the checklists Apollo astronauts wore on their sleeves. Every stop on the card has a latest time to leave, like the Apollo walk-back limit.

Factors I considered
- Safety first: Suit oxygen with a reserve, a maximum time in the suit, return before sunset, never crossing ground steeper than 25°, and the time to walk home from every point on the map.
- Communication: Radio line of sight to the habitat, so the crew knows where they would be out of contact.
- Checking against reality: Elevation, sun position, oxygen and radiation were each compared with NASA measurements or NASA reference values.
- Readability for the crew: Yellow with a black edge for the route (readable for colour-blind users), magenta for science stops, amber and red only for cautions and warnings, a cyan helmet display that stands out against Mars's orange ground, and a black-on-white card that prints without colour.
- Science value: Stops are suggested where orbit sees minerals that record water, such as clays and hydrated sulfates.

I hope that the first walk on Mars can be planned with the best data we have today, so everyone who steps out on Mars comes home, with stories to tell.

in this project i used HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no build step), Leaflet, three.js and Web Workers for the app; Python with NumPy, rasterio, SciPy, scikit-image, Pillow and Matplotlib for the data pipeline; PyTorch and segmentation_models_pytorch on Google Colab for the AI model; GitHub Pages for hosting.
